title: DeepSeek 超级智能体：以注意力预算驱动的编程智能体
author: Muhammad Saud
content:
DeepSeek's super-agent is an open-source coding-agent prototype released on 31 October 2026 that runs background coding sessions against a single GitHub repository. Instead of optimising for benchmark scores, its design optimises for human attention: every interaction with a developer costs budget, and the whole system is built to spend that budget sparingly.

Key takeaways

  • On 31 October 2026, DeepSeek's Harness team open-sourced dsh-superagent-prototype under the MIT licence: a proactive coding agent that works a single GitHub repository in parallel background sessions.

  • The headline idea is not a new model but a new constraint. The design minimises the human attention each autonomous action costs, instead of maximising benchmark pass rates.

  • The architecture is a two-layer router-worker design built from five primitives (Sources, Triggers, Threads, Mandates, Tickets), with a stateless evaluator and immutable mandates that bound each worker's authority.

  • Each worker session runs in an isolated git worktree. Shell commands longer than five seconds move to the background automatically and are killed after a hard thirty-minute cap.

  • The catches are real: workers run shell commands as your OS user with no approval prompt, DeepSeek published no independent benchmarks, and the README states it is a research prototype, not a finished product.

What did DeepSeek actually release?

On 31 October 2026, DeepSeek's Harness team published a repository called dsh-superagent-prototype on GitHub under the MIT licence. It is a proactive coding agent packaged as a bundle for DeepSeek Harness, the company's plugin-oriented agent framework. Point it at one GitHub repository, and it listens to issues, pull-request comments and webhooks (plus, optionally, the Chinese workplace chat tool Feishu). When an allowed person asks for work, the agent opens a work item, runs in its own session and working directory, and answers in the original conversation, for example by opening a pull request.

Alongside the code, the Harness team published a technical article titled "Super-agent Design Exploration: Toward More Autonomous Agent Systems" (via a WeChat post on 31 October, reported by Tech in Asia). Its argument: mainstream agents run in isolated sessions, so multi-task collaboration is capped by human attention. The super-agent moves session management into the system and reserves humans for decisions.

According to DeepSeek, an internal instance has been running continuously: reproducing and fixing bugs, responding to code reviews, and iterating on DeepSeek Harness itself. The company stresses the open-sourced code is a research prototype for reference, not an official product, and differs from the internal system. It may contain bugs.

How does the super-agent's router-worker design work?

The design documents in the repository (docs/000-philosophy.md and docs/001-domain.md, analysed by Reid Marlow) describe a two-layer architecture: a main session with a small tool set routes, while dedicated worker sessions code. The pieces that matter:

The five primitives

The domain model separates event streams from permissions with five concepts: Sources, Triggers, Threads, Mandates and Tickets. A Source (GitHub notifications, issue webhooks) emits immutable Triggers into an ordered Thread. A stateless Eval component checks each Trigger against repository policy and decides whether to create a Ticket. An accepted Ticket receives an immutable Mandate fixing its scope and operational strength.

Stateless evaluation

Most multi-agent frameworks keep pending queues, retry timers and polling loops inside the planning agent. DeepSeek rejected internal scheduler state entirely: Eval holds nothing between runs, takes a batch of Triggers, evaluates them against policy, and decides immediately. Waiting on an external event (code-review approval, CI pipeline) is modelled as an ordinary event Source; when the event occurs, it emits a Trigger that enters the pipeline naturally. The payoff is restart safety: after a mid-deployment restart, the Source recovers its read position from git history and webhook offsets.

Subscriptions that cannot widen authority

Context delivery is separated from permission checks through subscriptions: a Ticket subscribes to the Threads it touches, so a PR comment or finished CI build fans out directly to the worker as context. This fanout bypasses the evaluator but cannot widen the Ticket's authority: the Mandate stays fixed. If a comment asks for out-of-scope work, the worker hands it back to the router instead of self-escalating, defending against conversational drift, where a bugfix quietly grows into a multi-file refactor.

Workers in git worktrees, with hard time limits

Each Ticket gets its own working directory, provisioned as an isolated git worktree. Any shell command running longer than five seconds moves to a background job automatically, so installs and test suites cannot block incoming messages. Background jobs face a hard thirty-minute cap, after which the runtime kills them and records the output in an audit trail. One media-reported internal test claims p95 completion of 15.7 minutes versus 29.5 for a single-session setup. DeepSeek published no formal benchmarks, so treat that as a company claim, not a verified result.

What is an "attention budget" and why is it new?

The design's most interesting idea is budgeting human attention the way other frameworks budget tokens or tool calls. Against real team repositories, developer fatigue is the primary failure mode: an agent posting twenty notifications, opening four draft pull requests and asking five vague questions burns more engineering time than writing the code by hand.

DeepSeek's answer is explicit human handoffs: the runtime never parses free-text transcripts to guess whether an agent needs help. An agent that needs a human writes to a structured attention field; the Ticket then waits, releases its worker slot, and posts a single structured question back to the original channel. A web panel shows only items requiring human action, keeping healthy tickets out of sight.

Policy changes get the same respect: updating rules mid-flight does not kill active Tickets immediately (which would leave dirty worktrees). Instead, a policy-change notification reaches the active assignment, letting the worker checkpoint or roll back cleanly before terminating.

What are the catches?

Before you point this at your production repository, know what the release notes actually say.

  • Workers run shell commands with no approval, as your OS user. The execution documentation states that worker sessions execute commands without approval directly as the operator's OS user. That is a serious trust decision for any engineering team: you are giving an experimental agent the same shell you have.

  • No benchmarks. DeepSeek explicitly provides no benchmark results for the prototype. The only performance numbers in circulation come from media reports of an internal test, not from a reproducible evaluation.

  • Single-repository scope. The prototype is designed for one GitHub repo at a time. Teams with dozens of services will need to run multiple instances or rethink the model.

  • It is a prototype. Roughly 97.5 percent TypeScript by bytes (per media analysis), grown out of DeepSeek's own daily work. The README warns it may contain bugs and is not identical to the internal system.

The hype metric, for the record: media reported roughly 2,000 stars and 170 forks within the first twelve hours. That measures interest, not quality.

Try the core idea in your own agents: a 40-line attention budget

You do not need DeepSeek's codebase to apply its best idea. An attention budget is a rate limit on human interruptions plus a scope guard, and both fit in plain Python 3:

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
import time

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Mandate:
ticket_id: str
allowed_paths: tuple[str, ...]
max_questions_per_hour: int = 2

def in_scope(mandate: Mandate, path: str) -> bool:
"""True only if the path stays inside the mandate's scope."""
return any(path.startswith(p) for p in mandate.allowed_paths)

@dataclass
class AttentionBudget:
asked: list[float] = field(default_factory=list)

def can_ask(self, limit: int) -> bool:

    now = time.time()

    self.asked = [t for t in self.asked if now - t < 3600]

    return len(self.asked) < limit


def ask(self, mandate: Mandate, question: str) -> str | None:

    # Returns ONE structured question, or None if the budget is spent.

    if not self.can_ask(mandate.max_questions_per_hour):

        return None  # budget exhausted: checkpoint instead of asking

    self.asked.append(time.time())

    return f"[{mandate.ticket_id}] {question}"




Example: the worker may touch src/payments only, and may ask twice per hour.

mandate = Mandate(ticket_id="T-42", allowed_paths=("src/payments/",))
budget = AttentionBudget()

if in_scope(mandate, "src/payments/refund.py"):
question = budget.ask(
mandate,
"Which refund policy applies to partial SEPA payments: v1 or v2?"
)
print(question or "Budget spent: checkpointing and waiting for a review event.")

The pattern generalises: scope checks separate from routing, explicit human-handoff paths instead of parsed transcripts, and asking a human as a budgeted operation. The super-agent's philosophy in miniature.

Why this matters for teams in Europe

For European teams, two things stand out. First, the MIT licence and self-hostable design let you run it on your own infrastructure, simplifying the EU data-sovereignty conversation around AI tooling. Second, the pain is universal: teams drowning in agent notifications. The attention-budget principle is the cheapest, highest-leverage idea in this release, and you can adopt it this week without installing anything from DeepSeek.

If you build agent infrastructure, read docs/000-philosophy.md and docs/001-domain.md in full. The value is in the plumbing: stateless evaluators, immutable mandates, subscription fanout, isolated worktrees. No model magic required.

summary: DeepSeek 推出了一套「超级智能体」框架，旨在解决智能体疲劳问题。与传统多智能体系统用大量通知和请求淹没开发者不同，该系统采用两层架构（路由层与工作层），包含五个核心原语：来源、触发器、线程、授权和工单。它采用无状态评估，仅通过结构化的注意力字段请求人类介入，而非从对话记录中猜测意图。每个工作单元在独立的 git worktree 中运行，并设有硬性时间限制，以防止对话漂移和资源失控消耗。

mainPoints.explanation: 该系统不以优化基准分数为目标，而是以最小化人类认知负担为优化方向，将开发者注意力视为类似 LLM 中 token 的有限资源。
评估器在多次运行之间不保留内部状态，依靠 git 历史和 webhook 来恢复智能体的位置，从而确保系统在重启时的安全性。
每个任务在独立的 git worktree 中运行，设有 5 秒的后台化阈值和 30 分钟的硬性上限，以防止无限循环或大规模重构。
该框架使用来源（输入）、触发器（事件）、线程（上下文）、授权（范围）和工单（任务）将事件流与权限分离。

keyQuotes: 核心思路不是新模型，而是一种新约束。
该设计像其他框架预算 token 或工具调用那样，为人类注意力做预算。
运行时从不解析自由文本对话记录来猜测智能体是否需要帮助。
需要人类介入的智能体会写入一个结构化的注意力字段。
